Rest the upper prong against the upper front teeth and the lower prong against the lower front teeth, with the lips slightly pursed to help steady it. With the index finger of the other hand, flick the free end of the reed so that it vibrates; the sound travels through the teeth into the mouth and nasal cavities. Beginners first keep the reed vibrating freely, then change the pitch by moving the tongue and adding a nasal tone; steady plucking with tongue movement produces fast rhythms. In Carnatic music the morsing often follows the syllable patterns of the mridangam, imitating drum strokes by blocking and releasing the airway with the tongue.

Similar forms exist under different names in many places, and may have spread along ancient trade routes between Asia and Europe, including the Silk Road.

The morsing is an idiophone related to the jew's harp, found mainly in Rajasthan in North India, in South Indian Carnatic music, in Nepal and in Sindh in Pakistan. Its frame is a horseshoe-shaped metal ring with two parallel prongs, and the metal reed in the middle is fixed at one end and free to vibrate at the other, the free end bent so that it can be plucked. It is held against the front teeth, steadied with one hand, plucked with the index finger of the other, and then the tongue and a nasal tone change the pitch. It belongs to the plucked idiophones, among the reed idiophones, and is used in Carnatic concerts, percussion ensembles and Rajasthani folk music, and has also appeared in Hindi films.
音色由金屬簧片振動經牙齒傳入口腔與鼻腔，可隨舌位與鼻音改變音高，快速彈撥能產生快: The timbre comes from the metal reed vibrating and passing through the teeth into the mouth and nasal cavities; it can be changed in pitch by the position of the tongue and by nasal tone, and fast plucking produces fast figures. Narrowing the mouth cavity produces a phase-shifter-like change of colour. The basic pitch can only be adjusted a little, usually downwards; raising it requires filing and may damage the instrument. It is close to the jew's harp of the same family, traditionally made of iron but also of brass, wood or bone; the sources do not clearly record how its volume is controlled.
